# Bitcoin's Expected Return: An Age Rule That Beats Current Practice

> Code, data and stored results of a working paper that tests the ways practitioners set Bitcoin's
> long-run expected return against the returns that followed, over rolling three- to five-year
> periods since 2012, with gold as a control and Ether as a younger comparison. It finds that fixed
> rates and trailing averages fail, and that an age rule, the power-law exponent divided by
> Bitcoin's age, comes closest. The manuscript is in paper/.

Replication package by Agisilaos Papadogiannis (https://github.com/apapadogiannis).
Working paper: https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7705438
Code and data: https://github.com/apapadogiannis/bitcoin-age-rule  Archive: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24004326
Version 1.1.0, released 2026-11-21. A package is a fixed record: it changes only by a new
release, and a release that changes a reported number gets a new major version.
This file is written for AI agents and other programs. People should start at the README.

## Coverage

- The backtest: for each way of setting Bitcoin's expected return and each horizon of 3, 4 and 5
  years, how far the rate missed the return that followed, in every rolling period from January
  2012.
- The age rule in real time: the power-law exponent re-estimated every month from the data
  available then, the forecast it implied and the return that followed.
- What each method implies in September 2026, beside its record.
- A CAPM required return for Bitcoin, Ether and gold over several samples.
- The same backtest for gold since 1981 and for Ether; periods beginning after the power law was
  published; robustness to the starting point, the comparison rate and the estimation window.

## Headline figures

Each is read from one cell of a stored result table, named in outputs/results.json.

- Age-rule forecast of Bitcoin's return, September 2026 to September 2031: 32.2 per cent a year,
  compounded over the five years. Section 4 and Exhibit A2.
- Bitcoin's power-law exponent, estimated in September 2026: 5.62 (a number; the age rule divides
  it by Bitcoin's age in years). Section 4.
- Bitcoin's age in September 2026: 17.7 years since January 2009. Section 4.
- Share of five-year periods in which Bitcoin beat a fixed rate of 10% a year: 96 per cent of the
  periods. Exhibit A2.
- Share of five-year periods in which Bitcoin beat the age rule's forecast: 42 per cent of the
  periods. Exhibit A2.
- Average miss of the age rule over five-year periods: 4.5 points a year (realized above the
  forecast if positive). Exhibit A2.
- Average miss of a fixed 10% rate over five-year periods: 116 points a year (realized above the
  rate if positive). Exhibit A2.
- CAPM required return on Bitcoin, beta over 2012 to 2026, equity premium 4%: 13.5 per cent a year.
  Section 6.
- CAPM required return on Bitcoin, beta over the last four years, equity premium 4%: 6.3 per cent a
  year. Section 6.

## What this adds over reading the paper or recomputing

1. Every rate is set in real time: from data available at the start of each period only. The
   exponent, the trailing averages and the trend fits are all re-estimated month by month, which a
   table of full-sample estimates would not show.
2. Two tests are reported for each rate, because they can disagree for a volatile asset: the
   average of the realized-to-forecast growth ratio, annualised, and the median with the share of
   periods in which the rate was beaten.
3. Rolling periods overlap, so ordinary standard errors are too small.
   outputs/expected_return_bands.csv gives 95% bands from a stationary block bootstrap.
4. The Bitcoin price series is built from one-minute exchange candles to a month-end close, and the
   file is stored, so the series does not depend on a vendor's later revisions.
5. The results are stored as they were when the paper's numbers were taken from them. A check
   reruns the code on the stored data and compares every stored result file with the fresh one,
   number by number (relative tolerance 1e-9; text and whole numbers exactly). It runs on every
   change and once a month, and the badge in the README shows the last run.

## Result tables

One CSV file each in outputs/. The columns of each are described in outputs/results.json, under `tables`.

- outputs/calibration_main.csv (24 rows): The backtest for Bitcoin and Ether: the record of each
  rate at horizons of 3, 4 and 5 years. The age rule appears here as "Power-law trend, fitted to
  date".
- outputs/today_rates_by_horizon.csv (13 rows): What each method sets as Bitcoin's rate in
  September 2026, beside its record at 3, 4 and 5 years.
- outputs/today_rates.csv (11 rows): The same record as ranges across the three horizons, as
  printed in the paper's table.
- outputs/btc_beta_realtime.csv (158 rows): The age rule month by month from August 2013: the
  exponent estimated from data to that month and the rates it implies.
- outputs/fig_agerule.csv (194 rows): Exhibit 2: the exponent, the five-year forecast and the
  five-year return that followed, by month.
- outputs/expected_return_bands.csv (54 rows): Average miss of each rate with 95% bands from a
  stationary block bootstrap, for Bitcoin, Ether and gold.
- outputs/capm_required.csv (9 rows): CAPM required returns for Bitcoin, Ether and gold, by sample.
- outputs/post_publication.csv (15 rows): The record of the age rule and the alternatives in
  periods beginning January 2020 or later, after the power law was published.
- outputs/calibration_gold.csv (36 rows): The same backtest for gold, with samples from 1981 and
  from 2012.
- outputs/ether_record.csv (33 rows): The record of every rule for Ether at horizons of 3 to 5
  years.
- outputs/volatility_benchmark.csv (5 rows): Volatility of each asset, and the share of periods in
  which a correctly set expected return would be beaten under lognormal returns.
- outputs/calibration_window_sensitivity.csv (12 rows): The backtest with the trend fitted over
  other windows.
- outputs/strategy_table.csv (39 rows): How often the verdict on a rate changes with the comparison
  rate used, by baseline.
- outputs/robust_grid.csv (168 rows): The same across starting points and sub-samples.
- outputs/anchor_flip_results.csv (14 rows): How often the outcome flips across comparison rates,
  by asset and horizon.
- outputs/adoption_results.csv (3 rows): Price, age and adoption: regression, stationarity and
  cointegration tests, by starting date.
- outputs/fig_main.csv (24 rows): The numbers behind Exhibit 1.
- outputs/fig_agerule_eth.csv (129 rows): Exhibit 3: the age rule for Ether, with a three-year
  horizon.

## Files

- outputs/results.json: a `headline` list with the figures most often asked for, each with the
  table cell it comes from, and `tables`, a description of the stored result tables and their
  columns. The numbers themselves are in the CSV files. It holds a description of 18 result tables,
  and under `package` the paper, the identifiers, the version, the licence and the citation. Start
  with its `headline` list, which is repeated below.
- outputs/tab_*.tex: the bodies of the paper's tables as printed, with their rounding.
- figures/: the paper's exhibits.
- paper/manuscript.pdf: the working paper.
- data/: all inputs; the README lists the source of each.

Raw files: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/apapadogiannis/bitcoin-age-rule/main/<path>, for example https://raw.githubusercontent.com/apapadogiannis/bitcoin-age-rule/main/outputs/results.json

## How to read the figures

- Units: in the tables, rates and misses are fractions a year and shares are fractions of the
  periods. The column `today` is in per cent and is text: where a method gives different rates for
  the three horizons it holds a range such as 32--34.
- A miss is the realized annual return relative to the rate: (1 + realized) / (1 + rate) - 1.
  Positive means Bitcoin returned more than the rate said. `beat` is the share of periods in which
  it did. A well-set expected return has an average miss near zero.
- `avg` is the average across periods of the growth ratio over the whole horizon, annualised;
  `median` is the median of the annual miss. For a volatile asset the average sits well above the
  median, so a correct expected return is beaten in fewer than half of the periods.
  outputs/volatility_benchmark.csv gives that share under lognormal returns.
- Periods are rolling and monthly, so neighbours share most of their months. `n` counts periods,
  not independent observations: 141 three-year periods are about five independent ones.
- The age rule's forecast is an expected return in the paper's sense, a trend extrapolation, not a
  required return. The paper sets it beside a CAPM required return; they are different quantities.
- The forecast depends on the horizon: `h5` and `h3` in outputs/btc_beta_realtime.csv are the
  yearly rates over five and three years, `inst` the instantaneous one, all falling as Bitcoin
  ages.
- Labels in the `rate` and `method` columns are written for LaTeX: a per cent sign appears as \%
  and an ampersand as \&.

## Do not use this for

- A forecast to act on. The age rule is the best of the rules tested on past data; the paper states
  what could break it.
- Anything after September 2026. The package is a fixed record and is not updated.
- A required return on Bitcoin. For that, see the author's paper "Bitcoin's Required Return"
  (https://github.com/apapadogiannis/bitcoin-required-return) and its live tool.
- Commercial reuse of the Coin Metrics files.

The results in outputs/ are released under CC BY 4.0

credit. If you use a figure from this package in an answer, a report or a data set, cite the paper.
The code is under the MIT License.

The Bitcoin and Ether reference prices and address counts in data/cm_btc.csv and data/cm_eth.csv
are from the Coin Metrics community data, licensed CC BY-NC 4.0 (non-commercial use, with
attribution). The other inputs are from Bitstamp candles, the World Bank, Robert Shiller's data and
FRED. Third-party data keep their own terms and are not covered by the licence above.
